questions.question: Which of these is the best prompt?

options.explanation: Too short: Claude has to guess what kind of game you want and for whom.

options.text: “Make a memory game that works in the browser for an 8-year-old. There are 12 cards, and the pictures are animals. Use only HTML, CSS and JavaScript.”
options.explanation: Great! The prompt says what, for whom and within which limits.

options.text: “Would you be so kind as to make something nice?”
options.explanation: Being polite is nice, but the request has no content.

questions.question: Your site has a bug. How do you ask for a fix?

options.explanation: Claude doesn’t know what’s wrong. Tell it what happened and what you expected.

options.text: I explain what I did, what happened and what I expected, and paste in the error message
options.explanation: Correct. That way Claude can get straight to the point.
Parts that work may break at the same time. First ask it to fix just this bug.

questions.question: Why is it worth writing limits into your prompt, for example “don’t change the design”?

options.text: So that Claude doesn’t change things that are already good
options.explanation: Exactly. Limits keep the changes where you want them.
The point of limits isn’t speed but making the result match your wishes.

options.text: There’s no point, Claude knows that anyway
options.explanation: Claude can’t know what you like unless you tell it.
